newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London kept early losses up to the close as aggressive hedge selling by the origins met with very little roaster buying interest. The downside was supported by some scale-down manufacturer buying at the lows. November lost $17 to close at $1,495 a tonne. In New York arabica futures closed higher and the December/March spread widened again to 5.15 cents/lb. This is due to tight nearby supplies caused by the lateness of the crops which is making the period of tight supplies stretched out longer than would otherwise have been possible and is making some roasters and traders uneasy. Trade sources said that there seems to be very little coffee available for October/November even at steep premiums. Under the ACPC retention plan there should be 500,000 bags less of Central American exports but this was to be offset by 1 million more bags from Colombia. However, it is not yet sure whether Colombia can fill the gap due to transport problems. It was said that whatever milds are available are being taken by European roasters who are outbidding US counterparts.

BRAZIL - Brazil's coffee farmers are looking ahead to 1997/98 and based on current flowerings, very early signs are that output in key states will be below the 1996/97 levels. However, a more precise assessment cannot be made before November, when the flowerings have begun setting, giving agronomists a more concrete idea of crop size. But the fact most regions will see an 'off' year in the crop cycle where there is a larger harvest every other year means even at this early stage, that agronomists expect a drop in output. Some predict falls of up to 50 percent in regions that have been hit by dry weather such as Espirito Santo and the Zona da Mata Region in Minas Gerais. Other traders are considering a worst/best case scenario of 21 to 24 million bags.

UNITED KINGDOM - UK broker GNI said it expects world coffee production in 1996/97 to fall short of consumption by 4.486 million 60-kg bags. In its October commodity perspective report. GNI said world production in 1996/97 is likely to reach 94.663 million bags, while consumption will climb to 99.149 million bags. GNI added the production shortfall will see world stocks fall to 21.4 million bags at the end of the period, down from almost 40 million bags two seasons ago. However, GNI forecasts that the recent trend of deficit production years will be halted in 1997/98, when production should climb to 103.3 million bags, compared with consumption of 100.6 million bags.

ICO - Coffee exports to all destinations by exporting members of the International Coffee Organization (ICO) during August 1996 totalled 5.460 million bags, down from 5.918 million bags exported the same month the previous year, preliminary ICO estimates show. This brought total exports in October/August 1995/96 up to 65.092 million bags, which compares to 59.234 million bags the same period in 1994/95. Brazil's market share in October/August 1995/96 dropped to 17 percent from 25 percent the same period last year, while Colombia's market share reached 15 percent, practically unchanged from last year. Indonesia's exports surged to 4.443 million bags, up from 2.641 million bags shipped the same period the previous year.

NORWAY - Norway imported 52,895 bags of coffee in August 1996, 13 percent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 513,100 bags, 25 percent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped sharply by 18 percent to 662,100 bags. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/August 1996 were Guatemala (71,600 vs 10,100 bags), Mexico (65,300 vs 54,300 bags), Brazil (104,300 vs 172,400 bags) and Colombia (111,300 vs 73,600 bags).
